doc.title: Loren Schoenberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2019

chapter: Benny Goodman and the big band
title: Becoming Goodman's personal manager; John Hammond and Buck Clayton
summary: Goodman's assistant quits, he becomes his manager, while his band gets gigs and charts, and John Hammond brings Buck Clayton.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: players and — it was about fifty percent young and fifty percent older, of course much — the old guys were younger than I am now. And so the band started to cotton. And in the meantime Goodman asked me to come back because this woman I had mentioned before, Muriel Zuckerman, who had been his Girl Friday, she quit, and he said, “Can you come in and just, until I find someone, answer the phones or just help with something?” So I started doing that, and then eventually when he found out that I knew musicians and I had a band, “Well can you recommend somebody?” And do you know, and he started to trust me. And then he started to say well you can go ahead and book the band, or can you write these checks, or can you answer this letter to so-and-so. What the hell? I mean it doesn’t take a lot of brains to write a letter you know. So I started, and I wound up becoming his personal manager I guess is what you would call it. Some people, you might question that. What does that mean, a personal manager? Benny Goodman didn’t have an agent. He didn’t need an agent. What happened in Benny Goodman’s office was he got a thousand offers a year to play. I mean people just calling him. He had no agent. It was just call the office of Benny Goodman, “Hello?” Yes I’m so-and-so from the Pori Jazz Festival in Finland and we’d like Mr. Goodman to play on August 9th and we can offer X amount of dollars. So I would assemble all the offers and he would pick which ones he wanted to do. We hired the band, and he had a travel agent. So this all started. Well in the meantime this band that I had put together, we started getting some gigs, I mean for $5 each or I would pay for it or something with the money I was making playing. And we started playing at a place called the Red Blazer Two which was on Third Avenue and 88th Street. And boy the band was really good and I was getting more charts. Johnny Carisi gave me some charts and then I had gotten to know Benny Carter through Ed Berger, and I got a handful of some copies of some Benny Carter charts, and just a whole bunch of other stuff. And early Ellington things at that time. And we made a record. And well and I want to mention one other name and it sounds like a storybook but it’s really true, John Hammond, who was Benny Goodman’s brother-in-law, and they were not talking and I can tell you about that if you’re curious about why that was. He was, you know, he was the guy — I mean he discovered Bruce Springsteen and George Benson and Aretha Franklin and all these people. I mean he brought them to fame. But at this time in the early 80s I mean, you know I mean he still loved big bands, he loved jazz and I guess in the 30s or 40s if John Hammond came to your gig that was you were going to be the next Count Basie or something like that. By 1980, in the early 80s, like who’s this old guy. Well he still loved big bands. And I met him, well through Goodman’s office because he wasn’t talking to Benny at that time and there were some things I had to work around. And I invited him to come hear the band. And he brought Buck Clayton with him. So then Buck started to give me music. And I want to be clear when I say give me music. © Fillius Jazz Archive -22-
